objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain certification, currency, records, privileges, medical rules and required documents from student pilot to flight instructor, and teach a learner to answer "am I legal and ready for this flight?" on their own, with the regulation for each answer.
why: Every learner you train will one day stand alone at the airplane and have to decide whether they may fly it. If you teach the rules as a list to memorize, they forget it; the AIH notes that pilots' memory of the regulations fades with the months since their last flight review [[25:92|AIH 3-41]]. On the checkride you must teach at least two of these knowledge elements, so you need both the rules and a way to teach them.

warmup: Think first: a private pilot calls you on Friday and asks, "Am I legal to take my kids flying on Sunday?" Before you answer, list every question you would ask her. Then ask yourself which of those questions are about the law and which are about whether she can actually fly that flight well.

key_terms.def: Where and when a pilot may fly, with whom, for what purpose and in what type of aircraft. [[1:31|PHAK 1-16]]
Restrictions the FAA places on a certificate when the pilot did not show every skill needed for all privileges of that level, category, class or type. [[1:31|PHAK 1-16]]
A signed written statement, usually by a CFI, that the holder received training in a specific area. [[1:31|PHAK 1-16]]
Having logged the minimum takeoffs, landings, approaches, flight reviews or other recent events that 14 CFR requires. [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]
The ability to manage the conditions expected on this flight. A pilot can be current and still not proficient. [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]
Month counting used for flight reviews, medicals and BasicMed: the period runs to the end of the last month, not to the same date. [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]] [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)]]

At least 1 hour of ground and 1 hour of flight training covering part 91 and the maneuvers the instructor judges necessary, required every 24 calendar months to act as PIC. [[60:236|14 CFR 61.56(a)]] [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]

A known condition, medication or treatment that would keep a pilot from meeting the standards for the medical certificate the flight needs. A pilot may not fly while it lasts. [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]]

Flying as PIC under 61.113(i) with a U.S. driver's license, a medical education course and a physician's exam instead of a current FAA medical certificate. [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)]] [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]]
Comprehensive Medical Examination Checklist: the part 68 form the pilot and a State-licensed physician complete for BasicMed. [[60:406|14 CFR 68.7]]
Kept in the aircraft where the pilot can produce it, as allowed for the pilot certificate, photo ID and medical certificate. [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)]] [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)]]
A teaching method that draws out the learner's knowledge through lead-off and follow-up questions while the instructor keeps control. [[25:116|AIH 5-13]] [[25:117|AIH 5-14]]

chunks.title: The question your learners must answer alone: "Am I legal and ready for this flight?"

body.p: Pilot qualification questions all reduce to one: may this pilot act as pilot in command (PIC) of this aircraft, on this flight, today? The RMH lists the pilot hazards in the order you will teach them: qualification (the right certificate and ratings), currency (the recent events 14 CFR requires) and proficiency (the ability to handle the flight) [[30:22|RMH 3-4]] [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]. Then come the aeromedical items: illness, medication, stress, alcohol, fatigue and emotion [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

body.p: Each certificate has privileges and limitations built into it, and other privileges and limits come from the aircraft and the kind of operation, under both part 61 and part 91 [[1:31|PHAK 1-16]]. So the same pilot can be legal for one flight and not for the next.

callout.text: How to teach it: do not open with a lecture of numbers. Give the learner a real flight they want to make and let them work the five questions out loud. A good scenario starts with a reason to fly, because a pilot's decisions change with the motivation to fly [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. Ask open-ended "how" and "why" questions; closed yes or no questions test only rote recall [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].
Five questions in order: Certificate and ratings, Currency, Medical and fitness, Documents, then Proficiency. Legal first, then ready.

check.q: Your learner answers "Am I legal?" by checking only the date of his flight review. Which three questions has he skipped?
check.a: Whether his certificate, ratings and endorsements cover this flight, whether his medical (or BasicMed) is valid for it and he is fit, and whether he has the required documents [[30:22|RMH 3-4]] [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)]]. Then he still has to judge proficiency [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

chunks.title: Certification and recordkeeping: what lasts, and what gets written down

body.p: Students often think a pilot certificate "runs out" like a medical. It does not. A pilot certificate, including a student pilot certificate issued after April 1, 2016, has no expiration date [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19(c)]]. A certificate without an expiration date stays valid unless it is surrendered, suspended or revoked [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19(a)(2)]]. What expires is the right to use it: currency and medical.

No expiration date [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19(d)(1)]]

Expires 24 calendar months from the month issued, renewed or reinstated [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19(d)(2)]]

body.p: Keeping a CFI certificate usable (recent experience, renewal and reinstatement) is taught in AI.II.K; this lesson does not repeat it. Two other certification rules catch pilots out:

bullets: Change of address: after 30 days from a move, the holder may not exercise certificate privileges until the FAA Airman Certification Branch has the new permanent mailing address [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]].

English: a student pilot applicant must be at least 16 (14 for a glider or balloon) and able to read, speak, write and understand English [[60:270|14 CFR 61.83]]. If a pilot does not meet the Aviation English Language Standard during a flight review, do not endorse it as complete [[12:8|AC 61-65K 11.4.2]].

body.p: Your part at the very start: a CFI may accept an application for a student pilot certificate, verify the applicant's identity and verify that the applicant meets 61.83 [[60:345|14 CFR 61.193(b)]]. The FAA encourages using IACRA; you register in the instructor role first [[12:12|AC 61-65K 16]]. After you complete the application in IACRA, the student can expect the card by mail in about 5 weeks [[12:13|AC 61-65K 18]], so start this on the first lesson, not the week before solo.

callout.text: Before processing a student pilot application you must check 61.83 eligibility and verify identity [[12:12|AC 61-65K 17]]. If the applicant does not meet age or English requirements, you still process it, marked as rejected, and send it on [[12:13|AC 61-65K 17]].

body.p: A pilot must record the training and experience used for a certificate, rating or flight review, and the experience used for recent flight experience [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(a)]]. Other flying need not be logged, but most learners will want it for insurance and their own records.

body.p: Solo time is only time as the sole occupant [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(d)]]. Training time is logged when received from an authorized instructor, and the instructor's entry must describe the training, give its length, and carry the instructor's signature, certificate number and expiration or recent experience end date [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(h)]] [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]]. How to word and sign those entries, and the records you must keep as an instructor, are in AI.II.K.

callout.text: Pilot certificate, medical certificate, logbook and other required records must be presented on reasonable request of the FAA, an NTSB representative, or a Federal, State or local law enforcement officer [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]].

How to teach it: at the end of an early lesson, hand the learner the pen. Have them fill in the logbook entry while you check it against 61.51(b), then you add the training entry. Within a few lessons they will catch missing items in your entry too.

check.q: You give a private pilot (ASEL) 1.3 hours of dual in a Cessna 172. She flies the whole time. Who may log PIC time?
check.a: Both. She may log PIC as sole manipulator of an aircraft for which she is rated [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(e)(1)]], and you may log PIC as the authorized instructor rated in that aircraft [[60:229|14 CFR 61.51(e)(3)]]. She also logs it as training received [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(b)(2)]].

chunks.title: Currency: the flight review and recent flight experience

body.p: Currency rules say what a pilot must have done recently to act as PIC. Teach them as a set of gates, each tied to one kind of flight.

head: Gate

rows: Flight review
A review given by an authorized instructor, plus the logbook endorsement, since the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month of the flight [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]
Any flight as PIC
Day passengers

3 takeoffs and 3 landings in the preceding 90 days as sole manipulator, same category, class and type (if a type rating is required); to a full stop in a tailwheel airplane if flying one [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)]]
PIC carrying persons
Night passengers
3 takeoffs and 3 landings to a full stop in the preceding 90 days, between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]]
PIC carrying persons in that night period
Instrument
6 approaches, holding, and intercepting and tracking courses within the 6 calendar months before the month of the flight [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]]
PIC under IFR or below VFR minimums
Instrument proficiency check
Required once more than 6 calendar months have passed without meeting 61.57(c) [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)]]
Getting IFR currency back
Recreational pilot, under 400 hours
Training and an endorsement if no PIC time in the preceding 180 days [[60:293|14 CFR 61.101(g)]]
Before acting as PIC again

bullets: No separate flight review is needed if, in the same period, the pilot passed a practical test or proficiency check [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(d)]] or completed a phase of the FAA pilot proficiency program (WINGS) [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(e)]].
A student pilot in training with a current solo endorsement needs no flight review [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(g)]].
The flight review may be combined with 61.57 recent experience at the instructor's discretion [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(h)]].
To regain landing currency, a pilot may fly as PIC under day VFR or day IFR with no persons or property on board other than those needed for the flight [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(2)]].

body.p: Calendar months versus days is the most common math error. Worked examples (dates computed in Python): a flight review on November 15, 2024 lets the pilot act as PIC through November 30, 2026, because November 2024 is the 24th calendar month before November 2026 [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]. Night landings to a full stop on August 1, 2026 plus 90 days reaches October 30, 2026 [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]]. Approaches flown in May 2026 keep the pilot IFR current through November 30, 2026 [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]].

callout.text: For ordinary small airplanes, passenger currency is by category and class: a pilot current in a Cessna 152 is legally current in a Cessna 172. The FAA still recommends currency and a checkout in each make and model before carrying passengers [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.3]].

How to teach it: draw a timeline on the whiteboard and have the learner place their own last flight review, last landings and last night landings on it, then read off the last legal day for each. Using their own logbook makes it application, not recitation.

check.q: A pilot made 3 night touch-and-go landings 20 days ago and 3 day full-stop landings last week. Can she carry a passenger at 2100, two hours after sunset?
check.a: No. Night passenger currency needs 3 takeoffs and 3 landings to a full stop in the night period within the preceding 90 days; touch-and-goes do not count and day landings do not count [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]].

bullets: Student pilot: no international flights except the listed Alaska training flights, and never contrary to limitations the instructor writes in the logbook [[60:278|14 CFR 61.89(a)]].

Sport pilot: the certificate lists no category or class; a logbook endorsement shows which aircraft the pilot may fly [[60:365|14 CFR 61.317]]. The MOSAIC rule removed the light-sport aircraft definition and replaced it with the 61.316 limits [[12:17|AC 61-65K 21]].

Sport night privileges need 3 hours of night training including a night cross-country with a landing at least 25 NM away, plus 10 full-stop night takeoffs and landings and an endorsement [[60:367|14 CFR 61.329]].

Recreational pilot: may fly solo outside these limits only to train for another certificate or rating, with a per-flight endorsement carried in the logbook [[60:294|14 CFR 61.101(i)]] [[60:294|14 CFR 61.101(j)]].

callout.text: A common trap: a 4-seat airplane may qualify under 61.316, but a sport pilot may still carry only one passenger [[60:365|14 CFR 61.316(a)(2)]] [[60:363|14 CFR 61.315(c)(4)]].

check.q: A recreational pilot wants to fly a friend to an airport 40 NM away that has a control tower. What does she need?
check.a: The 50 NM distance is allowed with the 61.101(b) endorsement for her departure airport [[60:292|14 CFR 61.101(b)]], but a towered airport needs the 61.101(d) training and endorsement, carried with her [[60:292|14 CFR 61.101(d)]] [[60:293|14 CFR 61.101(d)(3)]]. One passenger is allowed [[60:292|14 CFR 61.101(a)]].

body.p: Ratings and endorsements add to or limit any certificate. Without the category, class and type rating (if a class and type rating is required), a pilot may not act as PIC carrying another person or for hire [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(c)]]. To serve as PIC at all, the pilot needs the rating or the training plus a solo endorsement in that aircraft [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(d)]].

bullets: Complex airplane: logged training and a one-time endorsement [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(e)]].
High-performance airplane (an engine of more than 200 horsepower): logged training and an endorsement [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]].
Tailwheel airplane: training in normal and crosswind takeoffs and landings, wheel landings and go-arounds, and an endorsement [[60:215|14 CFR 61.31(i)]].

body.p: The endorsement wording for each of these is in AI.II.K. Here, make sure your learner can say which endorsement a given airplane needs before they ask to rent it.

callout.text: As a CFI, you may not endorse a flight review unless you conducted it under 61.56(a), and you may not endorse an instrument proficiency check unless you tested the pilot under 61.57(d) [[60:347|14 CFR 61.195(d)(5)]] [[60:347|14 CFR 61.195(d)(6)]].

How to teach it: give the learner three made-up job offers (a cost-shared trip, a free ride to a business meeting, a paid photo flight) and ask which certificate each one needs and why. Comparing similar cases builds correlation, not memorized lists.

check.q: You flew 3.0 and 2.5 hours of dual this morning. A student asks for a 3-hour cross-country lesson this afternoon. What limits you?
check.a: A flight instructor may not conduct more than 8 hours of flight training in any 24 consecutive hours [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]]. 3.0 + 2.5 = 5.5, so only 2.5 more hours remain; split or reschedule the lesson.

chunks.title: Medical certificates: class, privileges and expiration

body.p: Students confuse two things: the class of medical they hold and the privileges they are using today. Duration depends on the operation, the class and the pilot's age on the date of the exam, and it always runs to the end of a calendar month [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)]].

body.p: Any class can be used for lower privileges once its higher privileges lapse, because the table gives each class a duration for each kind of operation [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)]] [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)]]. Worked example (computed in Python): a commercial pilot who was 35 at a second-class exam on January 20, 2026 may use commercial privileges through January 31, 2027 and private privileges through January 31, 2031.

body.p: A sport pilot using a driver's license must follow its restrictions, must not have been denied at the most recent medical application, must not have had the last medical suspended or revoked, and must not know of a condition that would prevent safe operation [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(2)]] [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(2)(iv)]].

callout.text: How to teach it: the AIM advises student pilots to see an Aviation Medical Examiner early in training to avoid wasted expense, and future professional pilots to apply for the highest class they might need [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]]. Say this on the first lesson, not after the student has 15 hours.
Count from the exam month, not the exam day. Age at the exam, not today's age, picks the row.

check.q: You are 44 and had a second-class exam on June 10, 2025. Today is October 27, 2026. As a CFI, may you act as PIC on a dual lesson with a pre-solo student?
check.a: Yes. Commercial privileges lapsed at the end of June 2026 (12th month), but for CFI duties as PIC the same certificate serves as a third-class medical through the end of the 24th month, June 30, 2027, because you were over 40 at the exam [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)]] [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(a)(3)(ii)]].

chunks.title: Temporary disqualifications: when a valid medical does not mean fit to fly

body.p: A medical certificate is a snapshot from the exam day. The pilot must judge fitness before every flight. A pilot who holds a medical may not act as PIC or required crew while they know or have reason to know of a condition that would keep them from meeting the medical standards, or while taking medication or treatment that has that effect [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]]. Pilots flying without a medical may not fly while they know of a condition that would make them unable to operate safely [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(b)]].

head: Temporary disqualifier
What the sources say
rows: Illness

Some conditions, such as acute infections, anemia and peptic ulcer, may be temporarily disqualifying [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]]. The safest rule is not to fly with any illness; if that seems too strict, ask an AME [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]]
Medication

No crew duty while using any drug that affects the faculties contrary to safety [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(3)]]. Antihistamines, blood pressure drugs, muscle relaxants and motion sickness drugs can have impairing side effects [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]]
Alcohol

Not within 8 hours of any drink, not while under the influence, and not at 0.04 alcohol concentration or more [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. The AIM advises 12 to 24 hours from bottle to throttle [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]]
Fatigue, stress, emotion
Fatigue may not show until serious errors are made; an emotionally upsetting event can make a pilot unable to fly safely until recovered [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]] [[34:182|AIM 8-1-1]]
Scuba diving
Wait at least 12 hours before flying up to 8,000 ft MSL after a no-decompression dive, and at least 24 hours after a decompression-stop dive or before going above 8,000 ft [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]]

body.p: The IMSAFE checklist turns these into six questions the learner asks before every flight [[30:23|RMH 3-5]] [[34:182|AIM 8-1-1]]. Alcohol aftereffects such as a hangover can be a hazard longer than 8 hours after drinking [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

callout.text: A pilot may not refuse a test or hide results: on request of an authorized law enforcement officer a crewmember must submit to an alcohol test, and the FAA can require test results taken within 4 hours after acting as crew [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(c)]].
How to teach it: model it. Say your own IMSAFE out loud on the ramp at the start of every lesson, including the times you cancel. Learners copy what you do far more than what you say.

check.q: Your student and her passenger made a dive this morning that needed decompression stops. She plans to cruise at 6,500 ft MSL in 14 hours. What do you advise?
check.a: Wait at least 24 hours after a dive that required a controlled ascent, even below 8,000 ft [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]]. 14 hours is not enough for either of them.

body.p: BasicMed lets a student, recreational or private pilot, or a CFI acting as PIC, fly without a current FAA medical certificate, under the conditions of 61.113(i) [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)]]. It does not cover commercial pilot privileges, which still need at least a second-class medical [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)]] [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.1.2]].

head: Pilot requirement
Rule
rows: Hold a U.S. driver's license and follow its restrictions
Have held an FAA medical certificate at any point after July 14, 2006
Complete the medical education course within the 24 calendar months before the flight and keep the completion certificate
Have a comprehensive medical exam by a State-licensed physician within the 48 calendar months before the flight, using the CMEC
Be under a physician's care for any diagnosed condition that may affect flying
The most recent medical may be expired or special issuance, but not suspended or revoked; the most recent application not completed and denied

head: Aircraft and flight limit (current rule)
Rule
rows: Aircraft authorized for not more than 7 occupants and not more than 12,500 lb maximum takeoff weight, with no more than 6 passengers
No part of the flight above 18,000 ft MSL, outside the United States (unless that country allows it), or above 250 knots indicated
Completed CMEC and course completion certificate available in the logbook

callout.text: The 2017 checklist in the figure, and AC 68-1A, still say 6 occupants, 6,000 lb and 5 passengers [[36:8|AC 68-1A 3.2]] [[36:13|AC 68-1A 5.1.1]]. The current rule is 7 occupants, 12,500 lb and 6 passengers [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]]. Teach the regulation.

bullets: BasicMed applies only to the PIC. A safety pilot who is not acting as PIC needs a medical certificate [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.1]] [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.2.1]].
A CFI acting as PIC may instruct under BasicMed [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)(vii)]] [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.2.2]].
BasicMed does not replace an instrument rating, IFR currency or an IFR-equipped airplane [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.3]].
The limits apply to the whole flight from takeoff to full-stop landing, even if another pilot on board holds a medical [[36:16|AC 68-1A 5.2.5]].
A passport is valid photo ID but cannot replace the U.S. driver's license for BasicMed [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.2]].

body.p: Worked example (computed in Python): a course completed February 14, 2025 is good through February 28, 2027, and a CMEC exam on September 30, 2022 ran out at the end of September 2026, 48 calendar months later [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(i)]].

check.q: A BasicMed pilot wants to take five friends in a 7-seat airplane with a 5,400 lb maximum takeoff weight, cruising at 17,500 ft. Legal under BasicMed?
check.a: Yes, on these limits: 7 occupants or fewer, 12,500 lb or less, 6 passengers or fewer, and at or below 18,000 ft MSL [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]]. The older AC 68-1A numbers (6 occupants, 6,000 lb) would have said no; they are out of date.

chunks.title: Documents pilots must have, level by level

body.p: Use the figure to show what the card proves: grade of certificate, ratings and limitations, and no expiration date. Then teach what else must be with the pilot. Every required pilot crewmember needs the pilot certificate (or temporary authority) and a listed photo ID in physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)]]. Accepted photo IDs include a driver's license, a government ID card, an Armed Forces ID, a passport, or an airport security area credential [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)]] [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)(v)]].

head: Pilot
Must have with them
rows: Every pilot using a medical
The medical certificate or other FAA-acceptable documentation, in physical possession or readily accessible [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]]
Student pilot on a solo cross-country
Logbook, student pilot certificate and other required records [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(2)]]
Sport pilot
Logbook or other evidence of the instructor endorsements on all flights [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(3)]]; the U.S. driver's license if it is the medical qualification [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)]]
Recreational pilot

Logbook with endorsements on solo flights beyond 50 NM from the training airport, in airspace needing ATC contact, between sunset and sunrise, or without the category or class rating [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(4)]]; the 61.101(b), (c) and (d) endorsements are carried in the aircraft [[60:292|14 CFR 61.101(b)]] [[60:293|14 CFR 61.101(d)(3)]]
BasicMed pilot
U.S. driver's license [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(c)(2)(xiii)]], kept in personal possession [[36:10|AC 68-1A 4.2]]; CMEC and course certificate available in the logbook [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(3)]]
Flight instructor

The flight instructor certificate or other acceptable documentation, in physical possession or readily accessible [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(d)(1)]]; a medical only when acting as PIC or required crew [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(c)(2)(viii)]]

callout.text: Present the certificate, medical, logbook or other required record on reasonable request of the FAA, the NTSB or law enforcement [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]].

How to teach it: before a solo cross-country, ask the student to lay out every document on the wing and say the rule that requires each one. Missing items are found on the ramp, not at the destination.

check.q: You will act as PIC on a dual lesson with a pre-solo student. You have your pilot certificate, CFI certificate and passport, but left your medical at home and have no driver's license with you. Legal?
check.a: No. As PIC you need a medical certificate in possession or readily accessible [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]]. BasicMed needs a U.S. driver's license, and a passport cannot replace it [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(c)(2)(xiv)]] [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.2]].

body.p: Currency asks, "Did I log the minimum events?" Proficiency asks, "Can I manage the conditions I expect on this flight?" A pilot can meet IFR currency with approaches flown five months ago and still lack the proficiency to fly low ceilings today [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

AC 61-98E tells pilots to treat 61.57 as minimums and adjust them for experience, operating environment, the airports used and the make and model. A pilot current only in light winds on long runways should get more practice in strong winds or on short runways before carrying passengers there, and may need instruction first [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.1]]. Night deserves extra care, because night is a small part of most pilots' flying [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.2]].

Use the Swiss cheese model to show why: each layer of defense has holes, and a greater level of proficiency makes it less likely that the holes line up [[30:48|RMH 6-5]]. Loss of control usually happens when pilots lack proficiency, which is why the FAA wants personal currency programs and training beyond regulatory minimums [[15:9|AC 61-98E 2.1.2]] [[15:10|AC 61-98E 2.1.2]].

bullets: Knowledge fades too: in one study, pilots' memory of the regulations was related to the months since their last flight review, and even skills that were automatic in training may not stay automatic after disuse [[25:92|AIH 3-41]].
Teach learners to use a personal checklist based on experience, currency and comfort level to decide whether they are prepared for a particular flight [[25:17|AIH 1-13]].
A day with good weather is a much better time to fly an unfamiliar airplane for the first time than a day with low IFR conditions [[25:7|AIH 1-3]].

callout.text: The most dangerous sentence a learner can say is "I'm legal." Legal is the floor. Ask the follow-up every time: "Legal for what conditions, and when did you last fly them?"

check.q: A pilot made his 3 landings last month in calm air at a 6,000 ft runway. Sunday's trip with passengers ends at a 2,400 ft strip with a gusty crosswind. Is he current? Is he ready?
check.a: He is current if the landings meet 61.57(a) [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)]]. He may not be proficient: AC 61-98E says to get more practice in stronger winds or on short runways before carrying passengers there, possibly with an instructor [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.1]].

chunks.title: Running a flight review that builds proficiency

body.p: The flight review is your best tool against the currency-only mindset. It is a training event in which proficiency is evaluated, not a practical test, and it may take more than the 1 hour of ground and 1 hour of flight minimum [[15:22|AC 61-98E 4.1.1]]. Do not plan it around the regulatory minimum; plan it around the proficiency the pilot needs [[15:22|AC 61-98E 4.1.2]].

head: Stage
What you do
rows: Before

Interview the pilot: what they fly, where, how much and how recently. Read the logbook for total time, time in type and recency [[15:24|AC 61-98E 4.2.1]] [[15:25|AC 61-98E 4.2.3]]. Agree on how the review will run and what counts as satisfactory [[15:25|AC 61-98E 4.2.4]]
Ground

Tailor the part 91 review to the pilot, and stress pilot deviation avoidance, automation competency and angle of attack awareness [[15:26|AC 61-98E 4.3.1]] [[15:26|AC 61-98E 4.3.2]] [[15:26|AC 61-98E 4.3.3]] [[15:27|AC 61-98E 4.3.4]]. Have the pilot do full 91.103 preflight planning for the flight [[15:27|AC 61-98E 4.3.5.2]]
Flight

Always include takeoffs, stabilized approaches to landings, slow flight, stalls, spin awareness, unusual attitude recovery and flight by reference to instruments, plus abnormal and emergency procedures, in a realistic scenario [[15:27|AC 61-98E 4.3.5.1]] [[15:28|AC 61-98E 4.3.5.4]] [[15:28|AC 61-98E 4.3.5.5]]
After
Debrief with a collaborative critique, satisfactory or not [[15:28|AC 61-98E 4.4]]. Replay, reconstruct, reflect and redirect [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]. Endorse or log as dual given, as covered in AI.II.K

body.p: You may teach during the review. Instruction that corrects a weak area does not stop a satisfactory outcome, as long as the deficiency is corrected [[15:28|AC 61-98E 4.3.5.6]]. For a satisfactory review, the pilot should fly the maneuvers to the ACS for the certificate held [[15:27|AC 61-98E 4.3.5.1]].

callout.text: Check yourself too: you need the category and class (and type, if needed) on your pilot certificate and the category and class on your instructor certificate, and you should get recent experience in an unfamiliar make and model before reviewing a pilot in it [[15:25|AC 61-98E 4.2.5]].

check.q: A 2,000-hour pilot says, "Just sign me off after an hour around the pattern." How does AC 61-98E guide your answer?
check.a: The review is built on proficiency, not minimums; you, the instructor, decide the total time needed [[15:22|AC 61-98E 4.1.1]], and it should include the critical maneuvers such as slow flight, stalls and unusual attitudes regardless of experience [[15:28|AC 61-98E 4.3.5.4]].

chunks.title: Risk: unfamiliar aircraft, flight displays and avionics

body.p: Accident rates rise for pilots with little or no time in the aircraft type flown [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.3]]. Pilots without much make and model experience who fly in challenging conditions face a greater risk of fatal accidents [[57:4|AC 90-109A 5f(2)]]. The risk runs both ways: moving down from fast, high-altitude airplanes to a light, high-drag airplane is as risky as moving up [[57:3|AC 90-109A 5c]].

The best training is in the specific airplane the pilot will fly, with a well-qualified instructor who has recent experience in that make and model; the second choice is the same make and model [[57:3|AC 90-109A 5f]]. The flowchart turns that preference into decisions your learner can follow.

head: Unfamiliar item
Risk
How to manage it
rows: Aircraft
Different speeds, handling, stall behavior and systems

A comprehensive checkout in each make and model and study of the POH or AFM [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.3]]; a conservative buildup of maneuvers and fewer people on board until familiar [[57:6|AC 90-109A 6a(3)]] [[57:7|AC 90-109A 6a(3)]]
Flight displays and avionics
Not knowing which modes are engaged or armed; confusion after a programming error
Specialized transition training for TAA from an instructor experienced with that equipment [[15:26|AC 61-98E 4.3.3]]; anticipate, act and verify with each input [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]
Automation
Over-reliance degrades manual skill; failing to step down to a lower level of automation
Practice manual flight and choose the level of automation for the workload [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]; know how and when to fly without it [[25:23|AIH 1-19]]

body.p: Understanding, not memorized button sequences, is what transfers: a learner who understands a process has an easier time with unfamiliar aircraft and new avionics [[25:61|AIH 3-10]]. This applies to you as well. Instructors flying a different airplane may have to manage an avionics suite for the first time, and that change brings stress and risk [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

callout.text: Application: no 61.31 endorsement covers a move from a round-gauge 172 to a glass-cockpit 172 of the same category and class [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(e)]] [[60:213|14 CFR 61.31(f)]]. The law is silent here; the risk is not. Teach the learner to treat new avionics as an unfamiliar aircraft.

check.q: Your club's new airplane has avionics you have never used. A renter asks you for a checkout in it tomorrow. What do the sources say you should do first?
check.a: Get trained and current in it yourself. The instructor should have recent experience in the make and model, preferably [[57:3|AC 90-109A 5f]], and TAA transition training should come from an instructor experienced with that equipment [[15:26|AC 61-98E 4.3.3]] [[15:25|AC 61-98E 4.2.5]].

chunks.title: How to teach it: delivering instruction on K1 to K4

body.p: On the checkride the evaluator asks you to deliver instruction on at least two of K1 through K4. These are knowledge topics, so plan a short ground lesson rather than a flight demonstration. Two methods fit well.

head: Method
How it fits this Task
rows: Guided discussion

The learner reads first, then you draw out their knowledge with a lead-off question and follow-up questions while you keep control [[25:116|AIH 5-13]] [[25:117|AIH 5-14]]. Structure: introduction (attention, motivation, overview), discussion, conclusion [[25:117|AIH 5-14]]
Scenario-based training
A realistic flight with a reason to fly. A good scenario is not a test, has no single right answer, no obvious answer, and promotes decisions [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]

head: Part of the lesson
Example for K1 (currency) and K3 (medical)
rows: Attention
"Last month a pilot here flew his family with an expired flight review. His insurer refused the claim." Keep any story short; personal stories help but can turn into war stories [[25:100|AIH 4-7]]
Objective
"You will be able to read your own logbook and medical and give the last legal day for each kind of flight."
Lead-off question
"Your medical says June 2025. What is the last flight you could make with it, and why?"
Development
Fill the duration table together, then the currency timeline, using the learner's own dates
Application
A scenario with a flight on a specific date, passengers, night and a cold medicine
Conclusion and check
Summarize the five questions; have the learner explain one answer back in their own words

bullets: Ask one idea per question, adapted to the learner's level, and focused on the decision [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].
Use paraphrasing and perception checks to be sure you and the learner understood the same thing [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].
Practice with another applicant playing the learner, then critique the session; role play is how instructors build these skills [[25:100|AIH 4-7]].

callout.text: Bring a blank logbook page, a sample medical with the date covered, and a calendar. Working real dates on paper shows the evaluator that your learner, not you, is doing the thinking.

check.q: Why is "Is a third-class medical good for 60 months?" a weak question to ask your learner?
check.a: It is closed and only tests rote recall [[25:103|AIH 4-10]], and the answer depends on age at the exam and the operation [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(3)]]. Better: "You were 41 at your exam last September. Walk me through how long it lets you fly as a private pilot."

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Counting calendar months as days
Learner says a June 10 flight review ends on June 10 two years later
Show that the review runs to the end of the 24th calendar month [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]; work three examples on a calendar
Using today's age for medical duration
A 42-year-old assumes 24 months on an exam taken at 39
The row is picked by age on the exam date [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)]]
Treating passenger currency as general PIC currency
Learner thinks he cannot fly solo after 90 days without landings
61.57(a) applies to carrying persons; he may fly solo day VFR to regain it [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)]]
Counting touch-and-go landings at night
Night currency claimed from touch-and-goes
Night landings must be to a full stop [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]]
Equating legal with ready
"I'm current, so I'm fine" before a gusty short-field trip
Teach currency as a minimum [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.1]] and use personal minimums
Old BasicMed numbers
Quotes 6 seats and 6,000 lb
Teach the current 61.113(i)(1): 7 occupants, 12,500 lb, 6 passengers [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]]
Medical valid means fit
Flies on a drowsy cold medicine because the medical is current
Wrong document as ID or medical
Passport offered in place of a driver's license for BasicMed
Passport is photo ID only [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.2]]

body.p: Instructor errors show up too: teaching the rules as a list, quoting a handbook line that a newer rule replaced, or signing a flight review after a set hour count without checking proficiency. Fix them by teaching from the current regulation, using scenarios, and evaluating against the ACS [[15:27|AC 61-98E 4.3.5.1]].

check.q: A learner says, "My flight review was May 3, 2024, so I'm legal until May 3, 2026." What is the correct last day, and how do you fix the idea?
check.a: May 31, 2026, the end of the 24th calendar month [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]. Have the learner count months, not days, on a calendar for this and two more examples.

scenario.title: "Am I legal for Sunday?" A returning pilot calls
scenario.setup: Today is Tuesday, October 27, 2026. Dana, a private pilot (ASEL) with 310 hours, calls you. She wants to fly her two children on Sunday, November 1, in the club's new Cessna 172 with a glass panel and autopilot; she trained and has always flown round-gauge 172s. Her last flight review was October 2, 2024. She was 45 at her third-class exam on June 10, 2025. Her last flight was July 20, 2026: three day landings. She mentions she is taking an antihistamine for allergies that makes her drowsy. She asks you to "just look at her logbook and tell her she's legal." You want her to work it out herself.

questions.q: Can Dana act as PIC on November 1 on her current flight review?
questions.a: No. A review in October 2024 is good through October 31, 2026, the end of the 24th calendar month (computed in Python) [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]. She needs a flight review before Sunday.

questions.q: Is her medical valid for the flight?
questions.a: Yes. She was over 40 at the exam, so for private privileges the third-class medical lasts through the 24th month, June 30, 2027 [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(3)]].

questions.q: Is she current to carry her children?
questions.a: No. July 20 plus 90 days was October 18, 2026 (computed in Python), so she needs 3 takeoffs and 3 landings before carrying passengers [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)]]. The flight review and recent experience can be done together at your discretion [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(h)]].

Antihistamines can impair alertness [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]], and she may not act as crew while using a drug that affects her faculties contrary to safety [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(3)]], or while medication keeps her from meeting the medical standards [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]]. She should not fly while drowsy and should ask an AME about it.

questions.q: She is legally fine in the glass-panel 172 once current. How do you manage the risk?
questions.a: No 61.31 endorsement is needed for the avionics, but accident rates rise with little time in type [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.3]]. Do the review in the new airplane with emphasis on automation competency [[15:26|AC 61-98E 4.3.3]], and get some solo time in it before taking the children [[57:7|AC 90-109A 6a(3)]].

questions.q: How do you teach this call instead of just answering it?
questions.a: Use her real flight as the scenario and ask open-ended questions so she finds each gap herself [[25:120|AIH 5-17]] [[25:103|AIH 4-10]], then close with a collaborative critique that ends in a plan [[25:136|AIH 6-5]].

skills.do: The ACS says you demonstrate how to "Deliver instruction on at least two of the elements specified in K1 through K4." The evaluator picks or accepts two elements, for example K1 currency and K3 medical, and watches you teach them as a short ground lesson: a clear objective, questions that make the learner work real dates and cases with the regulation for each answer, correct current rules (not outdated handbook lines), and a check that the learner understood [[25:117|AIH 5-14]] [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].
skills.practice: Prepare a 10-minute lesson for each of K1, K2, K3 and K4 with one scenario each. Teach two of them to another applicant who plays a confused learner, time yourself, and have them critique whether every number you used came with its regulation.

quiz.q: A plastic student pilot certificate issued in 2026 expires:
options: Never; it has no expiration date
24 calendar months after issue
60 calendar months after issue
When the student's medical expires
quiz.why: Pilot certificates, including student certificates issued after April 1, 2016, are issued without an expiration date [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19(c)(1)]].

quiz.q: How many passengers may a sport pilot carry in a 4-seat airplane that meets 61.316?
options: None
One
Two
Three
quiz.why: A sport pilot may not carry more than one passenger [[60:363|14 CFR 61.315(c)(4)]], even though airplanes under 61.316 may have up to four seats [[60:365|14 CFR 61.316(a)(2)]].

quiz.q: A recreational pilot with 250 hours has logged no PIC time for 7 months. Before acting as PIC he needs:
options: Nothing; he has a current flight review
3 takeoffs and landings solo
Flight training and a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor
A new practical test
quiz.why: A recreational pilot under 400 hours with no PIC time in the preceding 180 days needs flight training and an endorsement [[60:293|14 CFR 61.101(g)]] [[60:294|14 CFR 61.101(g)]].

quiz.q: You give dual to a private pilot who acts as PIC. What medical do you need?
options: Second-class, because you are paid
Third-class
None
BasicMed
quiz.why: No medical is needed to exercise CFI privileges when not acting as PIC or a required crewmember [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(b)(7)]].

quiz.q: Under 91.17, a crewmember may not fly with an alcohol concentration of:
options: 0.02 or greater
0.04 or greater
0.08 or greater
Any amount above zero
quiz.why: The limit is 0.04 or greater in blood or breath [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)(4)]].

quiz.q: Under the current BasicMed rule, the maximum certificated takeoff weight of a covered aircraft is:
quiz.why: Not more than 12,500 lb, with not more than 7 occupants and 6 passengers [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]]. AC 68-1A's 6,000 lb is out of date.

quiz.q: A student pilot may log PIC time only when she:
options: Is at the controls with an instructor on board
Is sole occupant, has a solo endorsement and is in training
Has passed the knowledge test
Flies a cross-country flight
quiz.why: All three conditions are required [[60:229|14 CFR 61.51(e)(4)]].

quiz.q: A recreational pilot must carry his logbook with endorsements on a solo flight that:
options: Stays in the local practice area
Goes more than 50 NM from the airport where he trained
Is made in daylight at a nontowered field
Uses a rental airplane
quiz.why: Beyond 50 NM from the training airport, in airspace requiring ATC contact, at night, or without the category or class rating [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(4)]].

quiz.q: A pilot is current in a Cessna 152. What does AC 61-98E say about carrying passengers in a Cessna 172?
options: It is illegal until 3 landings in the 172
It is legal, but the FAA recommends currency and a checkout in each make and model first
It requires a 61.31 endorsement
It requires a flight review in the 172
quiz.why: Basic currency applies by category and class for non-high-performance small aircraft, but the FAA recommends currency in each make and model and a checkout from an instructor [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.3]].

quiz.q: In an AIH study, pilots' memory of the regulations was related to:
options: Their total flight hours
The months since their last flight review
The class of medical they held
Their age at certification
quiz.why: Memory of regulation details was related to the number of months since each pilot's last flight review [[25:92|AIH 3-41]].

final_quiz.q: Today is October 27, 2026. A pilot's flight review was signed October 2, 2024. He wants to fly solo as PIC on November 3, 2026. May he?
options: Yes, the review is good until October 2, 2026 plus a grace month
No; the review was good only through October 31, 2026
Yes; solo flights do not need a flight review
Yes, if he made 3 landings in the last 90 days
final_quiz.why: The review must be since the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month of the flight; for November 2026 that is November 2024 [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]. October 2024 plus 24 calendar months ends October 31, 2026 (computed in Python).

final_quiz.q: You are a CFI, 44 at your second-class exam on June 10, 2025. Today is October 27, 2026. Which may you do?
options: Act as PIC giving dual, and fly a paid sightseeing ride
Act as PIC giving dual, but not fly a paid sightseeing ride as PIC
Neither; the medical has expired
Only instruct pilots who act as PIC
final_quiz.why: Commercial privileges lapsed at the end of June 2026 (12th month) [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)]]; for CFI duties as PIC the certificate lasts to the 24th month, June 30, 2027 [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(2)]] [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(a)(3)(ii)]].

final_quiz.q: A private pilot made 3 night full-stop landings on July 25, 2026 and 3 night touch-and-goes on September 30. Tonight, October 27, she wants a passenger 1.5 hours after sunset. Legal?
options: Yes, the touch-and-goes renewed it
Yes, the July landings are within 6 calendar months
No; the full-stop landings are more than 90 days old and touch-and-goes do not count
No; night currency needs 5 landings
final_quiz.why: July 25 plus 90 days is October 23 (computed in Python); night currency needs full-stop landings in the night period [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]].

final_quiz.q: An instrument pilot last flew approaches, holding and tracking in May 2026 and nothing since. What is the last month she may regain currency with a safety pilot instead of an instrument proficiency check?
options: November 2026
December 2026
May 2027
November 2027
final_quiz.why: She is current through November 2026 [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]]. After more than 6 more calendar months, only an IPC restores it [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)]], so May 2027 is the last month (computed in Python).

final_quiz.q: A BasicMed pilot finished the course on February 14, 2025 and had his CMEC exam on September 30, 2022. Today is October 27, 2026. May he act as PIC under BasicMed?
options: Yes, both items are current
No; the course has run out
No; the exam is more than 48 calendar months old
Yes, if his old medical was valid after 2006
final_quiz.why: The exam must be within the 48 calendar months before the flight; it ran out at the end of September 2026 [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(i)(D)]]. The course is good to February 2027 [[60:207|14 CFR 61.23(c)(3)(i)(C)]].

final_quiz.q: Which BasicMed flight is NOT allowed?
options: 6 passengers in a 7-seat, 6,800 lb airplane
Cruise at 17,500 ft MSL
Cruise at 19,000 ft MSL
An IFR flight by an instrument-current pilot
final_quiz.why: No part of the flight may be above 18,000 ft MSL [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(2)]]. The other three are within 61.113(i)(1) and AC 68-1A 5.2.3 [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.3]].

final_quiz.q: A sport pilot flying on her driver's license asks for night privileges. What does she need?
options: Only the night training and endorsement
Night training and endorsement, plus a medical certificate or the BasicMed conditions
A private pilot certificate
Night is never allowed for sport pilots
final_quiz.why: 61.329 requires 3 hours of night training with a 25 NM night cross-country and 10 full-stop night takeoffs and landings, an endorsement, and a part 67 medical or the 61.113(i) conditions [[60:367|14 CFR 61.329]].

final_quiz.q: A recreational pilot plans a 35 NM trip with one passenger to a towered Class D airport. What does she need beyond her certificate?
options: Nothing, it is within 50 NM
The 61.101(d) training and endorsement for towered airports, carried with her
A private pilot certificate
A third-class medical
final_quiz.why: Class B, C or D airspace and towered airports need 61.101(d) training and an endorsement carried in the aircraft [[60:292|14 CFR 61.101(d)]] [[60:293|14 CFR 61.101(d)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner did a no-decompression scuba dive this morning and wants to fly a local flight at 3,500 ft MSL in 8 hours. What do you advise?
options: Fine; the limit only applies above 8,000 ft
Wait at least 12 hours after the dive
Wait at least 24 hours
Fine if she feels well
final_quiz.why: At least 12 hours before flying up to 8,000 ft after a dive without a controlled ascent [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

final_quiz.q: You will act as PIC with a pre-solo student. You carry your pilot certificate, CFI certificate and passport; your medical and driver's license are at home. Are you legal?
options: Yes, the passport is valid photo ID
Yes, a CFI never needs a medical
No; as PIC you need a medical, or a U.S. driver's license for BasicMed
Yes, under BasicMed
final_quiz.why: The PIC needs a medical in possession or readily accessible [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]], and BasicMed needs a U.S. driver's license, which a passport cannot replace [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(c)(2)(xiv)]] [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.2]].

final_quiz.q: A renter asks you for a flight review in the club's glass-cockpit airplane, which you have never flown. What does AC 61-98E say?
options: Any CFI with the rating may give it
Get recent experience or knowledge of that aircraft's limitations, characteristics and performance first
Do the review in a round-gauge airplane instead
Only a DPE may give it
final_quiz.why: For an aircraft in which the instructor is not current or familiar, get recent flight experience or sufficient knowledge first [[15:25|AC 61-98E 4.2.5]].

final_quiz.q: During a flight review the pilot's stall recoveries are weak. You teach, and she then flies them to the ACS. Can the review be satisfactory?
options: No; any weak item means unsatisfactory
Yes, as long as the deficiencies are corrected
Only if she flies another full review later
Only with an IPC
final_quiz.why: Instruction during the review does not prevent satisfactory completion if the deficiencies are corrected [[15:28|AC 61-98E 4.3.5.6]].

final_quiz.q: A commercial pilot without an instrument rating is asked to fly a paying passenger at night 30 NM to another airport. What does his certificate allow?
options: It is allowed; the flight is under 50 NM
It is prohibited, because carriage of passengers for hire at night is prohibited without the instrument rating
It is allowed with a second-class medical
It is allowed under BasicMed
final_quiz.why: The limitation prohibits carriage of passengers for hire on cross-country flights over 50 NM or at night [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(b)(1)]]. Whether the trip also needs an operating certificate is a separate question (CA.I.A).

takeaways: Teach one question in five parts: certificate and ratings, currency, medical and fitness, documents, then proficiency.
Pilot certificates do not expire; currency and medical privileges do, mostly by calendar month.
Medical duration depends on class, the operation and age on the exam date; a higher class steps down to lower privileges.
A valid medical never overrides 61.53 and 91.17: fitness is decided before every flight.
BasicMed today: 7 occupants, 12,500 lb, 6 passengers, 18,000 ft and 250 knots; teach the regulation over AC 68-1A.
Currency is the legal floor. Run flight reviews and checkouts to build proficiency, especially in unfamiliar airplanes and avionics.
Use scenarios and open questions so the learner, not you, answers "am I legal and ready?"
cfi_notes: Outdated: AC 68-1A (2017) 3.2, 5.1.1 and 5.2.1, and the CMEC form in its Appendix A, still say BasicMed aircraft are limited to 6 occupants, 6,000 lb and 5 passengers. Current 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) says 7 occupants, 12,500 lb and 6 passengers. AC 68-1A also says the exam must be within 48 months; 61.23(c)(3)(i)(D) now says 48 calendar months. Teach the CFR.

Outdated: AC 68-1A 4.1.4 says sport pilots may not operate under BasicMed, and 3.2 lists "may not fly for compensation or hire" under 61.113(i)(2)(i). The current 61.329(b) and 61.23(c)(1)(vi) let a sport pilot use the 61.113(i) conditions for night flight, and the current 61.113(i)(2) lists only the altitude, outside the United States and 250 knot limits. Compensation is still controlled by the certificate held (61.113(a) to (h)), and commercial privileges still need a second-class medical (61.23(a)(2)).

Outdated: PHAK 1-16 says a sport pilot flies a light-sport aircraft in daytime. Since MOSAIC, the light-sport aircraft definition is gone (AC 61-65K 21), aircraft limits are in 61.316, and night is allowed with 61.329.

Outdated: PHAK 1-17 says a recreational applicant must obtain a third-class medical; 61.101(k) now allows BasicMed. PHAK 1-18 says commercial pilots without an instrument rating are restricted to daytime flight within 50 NM when flying for hire; 61.133(b)(1) actually prohibits carrying passengers for hire on cross-country flights over 50 NM or at night. AIM 8-1-1a(1) says all pilots except glider and balloon pilots must hold medical certificates; sport pilots on a driver's license and BasicMed pilots are exceptions under 61.23(c).

The sources do not define how to count "preceding 90 days" to the day. This lesson counts the landing date plus 90 days as the last day; teach learners to leave a margin rather than argue the last day.

Point learners to AI.II.K for endorsement wording, solo endorsements, instructor records and CFI recent experience, and to CA.I.A for pilot-for-hire versus operator questions; this lesson only sets up those topics.

Many learners hold the paper habit that a CFI certificate "expires every two years." Certificates issued on or after December 1, 2024 have no expiration date (61.19(d)), but instructing still needs recent experience under 61.197. Be ready to explain both.
When a learner says "I'm legal," make the follow-up question a habit: "Legal for what conditions, and when did you last fly them?" It moves them from currency to proficiency without a lecture.

If a learner discloses a medical condition or medication to you, do not rule on it yourself. The AIM sends pilots to an AME, and 61.53 puts the duty on the pilot. Your job is to make sure they understand that duty.
gaps: Which specific medications or conditions are acceptable for flight is not listed in these sources; the AIM sends pilots to an Aviation Medical Examiner.
Club, school and insurance checkout requirements for a make and model, or for new avionics, are not in 14 CFR or the handbooks; they come from the operator and the insurer.
Avionics modes, annunciations and failure behavior come from the POH/AFM supplements and the manufacturer's guide, not from these sources.

No source here explains exactly how the 2024 BasicMed changes affect paid flight instruction beyond AC 68-1A 5.2.2.2; check current FAA BasicMed guidance before advising a CFI who teaches under BasicMed.
Whether a particular aircraft meets 61.316 (VS1, seats, prop and gear) comes from that aircraft's own documents; the regulations give only the limits.

activities.title: What the certificate card shows
activities.intro: Drag each description to the pin on the certificate that matches it.

pins.label: Must match the name on your photo ID
The grade of certificate the holder may exercise
The only date printed; there is no expiration date
Where Airplane Single-Engine Land is listed
Where a no-instrument passenger-for-hire restriction would appear

activities.why: Pilot certificates carry no expiration date [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19(c)]]. The back lists ratings and any limitations [[1:31|PHAK 1-16]], such as the commercial no-instrument limitation [[60:322|14 CFR 61.133(b)(1)]]. The certificate is carried with a photo ID [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)]].

activities.title: Which medical qualification does this flight need?
activities.intro: Sort each pilot by the least medical qualification the regulations require.

items.t: Commercial pilot flying a paid banner tow
Private pilot flying friends and sharing costs
CFI acting as PIC with a pre-solo student
Private pilot taking the commercial practical test in an airplane
Sport pilot flying by day in an airplane that meets 61.316
Student pilot training for a sport pilot certificate, by day
CFI giving dual to a private pilot who acts as PIC
Ground instructor teaching a weekend ground school

activities.why: Commercial privileges need second class [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23(a)(2)]]. Private, CFI as PIC and practical tests need third class unless under 61.113(i) [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(a)(3)]]. Sport pilot and sport student operations allow a driver's license [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)]]. A CFI not acting as PIC and a ground instructor need none [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(b)(7)]] [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23(b)(8)]].

activities.title: Work the numbers a CFI checks
activities.intro: Use the regulation in each question.

items.q: A recreational pilot with 220 hours last logged PIC time on April 15, 2026. Today is October 27, 2026. How many days ago was that?
items.why: From April 15 to October 27, 2026 is 15 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 31 + 30 + 27 = 195 days (computed in Python). That is more than 180, so he needs training and an endorsement [[60:293|14 CFR 61.101(g)]].

items.q: Since 0700 you have given 1.8 and 3.4 hours of dual. How many more hours of flight training may you give before 0700 tomorrow?
items.why: Limit 8 hours in any 24 consecutive hours [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]]. 8 - (1.8 + 3.4) = 2.8 hours (computed in Python).

items.q: A BasicMed pilot's airspeed indicator reads in mph. About what mph equals the 250-knot BasicMed limit? Round to the nearest mph.
A pilot's last 3 night full-stop landings were on July 20, 2026. Tonight is October 27, 2026. How many days ago were they?
items.why: 11 + 31 + 30 + 27 = 99 days (computed in Python), more than the 90 days 61.57(b) allows for carrying passengers at night [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]].

items.q: A sport pilot and one passenger fly a trip with $230 of fuel, oil and rental. What is the least the sport pilot must pay, in dollars?
items.why: A sport pilot must pay at least half the operating expenses [[60:363|14 CFR 61.315(b)]]: 230 / 2 = 115 dollars.

activities.title: Put the flight review in order
activities.intro: Order the steps of the AC 61-98E sample flight review checklist.
steps: Preflight review actions: scheduling, expectations, aeronautical history, part 91 and cross-country assignments
Ground discussion: English standard, regulations, the flight plan, risk management and personal minimums
Conducting the flight: basic skills, takeoffs and landings, slow flight, stalls, unusual attitudes, instruments, ADM, automation failures
Postflight discussion: replay, reflect, reconstruct, redirect
Aeronautical health maintenance and improvement plan
activities.why: These are Steps 1 to 5 of the AC 61-98E Appendix D sample checklist [[15:39|AC 61-98E Appendix D]].

activities.title: True or false: currency, proficiency and fitness
activities.intro: Your learners make these claims. True or false?

cards.s: If I meet 61.57, I am proficient for any passenger flight.
cards.why: 61.57 is a minimum to adjust for winds, runways, environment and make and model [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.1]].

cards.s: A current medical certificate means I may fly today even with a fever.
cards.why: A known condition that keeps you from meeting the standards grounds you [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53(a)]]; the safest rule is not to fly with any illness [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]].

cards.s: A pilot may be IFR current and still not proficient for low ceilings.
cards.why: Currency events done five months ago may leave the pilot without the proficiency for the flight [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

cards.s: My pilot certificate expires if I do not fly for two years.
cards.why: It has no expiration date [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19(c)]]; the flight review lapses instead [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]].

cards.s: Completing a WINGS phase can take the place of a flight review.
cards.why: One or more phases of an FAA-sponsored pilot proficiency program in the period meets the requirement [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(e)]].

cards.s: Eight hours after my last beer I am always safe to fly.
cards.why: 8 hours is the legal minimum [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]], but a pilot may still be under the influence; the AIM advises 12 to 24 hours [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].

activities.title: A renter moves to the new glass cockpit
activities.intro: A 400-hour private pilot, current in the club's round-gauge 172s, wants to rent the new glass-cockpit 172 next weekend for a night trip with his family. You run the checkout. Choose what you would do at each point.

steps.s: He asks whether he even needs a checkout, since it is "just a 172."
options: No checkout; he is current in category and class
A checkout in this make and model, with emphasis on the avionics, before he carries passengers
Only a 61.31 high-performance endorsement
Only a flight review
steps.why: Legally no endorsement is needed, but the FAA recommends a comprehensive checkout and currency in each make and model [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.3]], and TAA transitions need specialized training [[15:26|AC 61-98E 4.3.3]].

steps.s: In cruise the autopilot turns off course after he changes the flight plan, and he starts pressing buttons.
options: Let him keep pressing until it works
Have him fly by hand or drop to a lower autopilot mode, then sort it out
Take the controls and fix it for him without comment
Turn off all the avionics
steps.why: When automation does not do what is expected, reduce the level of automation, fly manually and take time to resolve it [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

steps.s: After 1.3 hours he flies well but is still slow with the avionics. He wants to keep the night family trip.
options: Approve it; he is legal
Suggest more day VFR time in this airplane before the night trip with passengers
Tell him he may never fly it at night
Approve it if he uses the autopilot the whole time
steps.why: Type clubs recommend significant day VFR time in a make and model before night or IFR [[57:4|AC 90-109A 5f(2)]], and a conservative buildup is a key mitigation [[57:6|AC 90-109A 6a(3)]].

steps.s: You check his logbook: his last night full-stop landings were 100 days ago.
options: Fine, night currency lasts 6 calendar months
He needs 3 night takeoffs and full-stop landings before carrying his family at night
He needs a flight review
He needs an IPC
steps.why: Night passenger currency needs 3 takeoffs and 3 landings to a full stop in the night period within 90 days [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]].

steps.s: After the checkout, what goes in his logbook?
options: Nothing; checkouts are not training
A training entry: what was covered, the time, and your signature, certificate number and expiration or RE end date
A 61.31 complex endorsement
A flight review endorsement
steps.why: Training received from an authorized instructor is logged with a description, the length, and the instructor's signature, certificate number and expiration or recent experience end date [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(h)]] [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]].
